cards.title: Don't reset the learning phase on a winning ad set
cards.summary: Protect performing ad sets from new-ad injections that reset sequencing and redistribute spend; only disrupt underperformers.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to add new ads into an ad set or campaign that is already hitting your KPI on Meta
steps: Check whether the ad set/campaign is hitting its KPI before touching it.

If it is hitting KPI, do not inject new ads into that ad set. Adding ads resets the learning phase and disrupts the sequencing Meta uses to distribute spend across existing creative, which risks breaking performance.
If it is missing KPI badly, treat it as open season: turn ads off, add as many new ads as you want. The source's reasoning is that a broken sequence is worth breaking because it isn't working anyway.

When you want more variations of a winning concept, do NOT pile them into the winning ad set. Build a separate ad set named for the same concept (e.g. 'concept one shoot two') so you can filter that they belong to one concept while keeping the original ad set untouched.
For the winning concept itself, scale by increasing budget rather than switching it off. The source calls turning off a winner to relaunch it in a scaling campaign a rookie mistake.
caveats: Source states this from personal experience of breaking a performing ad set years earlier.
The sequencing mechanic and learning-phase behaviour are Meta-specific and can change as the algorithm changes.

cards.title: Amount spent as the top creative performance proxy
cards.summary: Rank creative by amount spent first, then roROAS/CPA, then CPC and CTR, then video hook and hold rates as diagnostics.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a creative report to decide which ads to keep, iterate, scale or kill
steps: Rank metrics in this reliability order: (1) amount spent, (2) roROAS or CPA, (3) CPC and CTR, (4) hook rate and hold rate for video.

Treat amount spent as the best proxy over extended periods because Meta sequences spend across ads and attribution goes only to the last ad. An ad with lower roROAS but double the spend of others is likely driving purchases elsewhere in the account and may be your top-funnel standout.
Check roROAS or CPA using 7-day click or incremental attribution to avoid last-click distortion.

Use CPC/CTR as a leading indicator, especially at the fringes. If your average CPC is around a threshold (the source uses a $3 CPC example) and no ad above it has ever been profitable, you can predict very-early-spend ads will never work because traffic is too expensive.

Use hook rate (people past 3 seconds) and hold rate (people past 15 seconds, though the source tracks several definitions) only as diagnostic tools for video. They don't correlate to conversion, but a bad hook rate tells you to swap the hook; a bad hold rate points at the bridge or body.
Combine metrics rather than relying on one before deciding to kill or iterate.
caveats: Hook and hold rate definitions vary; the source uses multiple definitions in their own reporting.
Thresholds like a $3 CPC are account averages, not universal benchmarks.

cards.title: CBO vs ABO is a risk-tolerance choice
cards.summary: CBO concentrates spend into few ads for higher ROI but more fatigue risk; ABO spreads spend to de-risk and manage product portfolios.
cards.use_when: Choosing campaign budget structure for a store, especially when running multiple products or when efficiency targets change
steps: Understand the mechanics: with CBO, the campaign distributes budget itself and Pareto's principle compounds — roughly 4% of ads can hold about 64% of total spend and revenue in the source's ad account breakdowns.
Accept the CBO trade-off: likely higher efficiency/ROI but higher risk. If those few ads fatigue, you have no backups.
Choose CBO if you need a quick efficiency spike and don't care about de-risking or testing right now.
Choose ABO-style manual control if you want a lower-risk steady state, more ads and products working, and protection against a single fatigue event.
For stores with a large product portfolio, avoid putting all products under one CBO, because spend concentrates into a few products (Pareto applies at product level too) and skews your assortment.
Note the source's own preference: they lean toward the lower-risk structure most of the time but switch to CBO in periods where efficiency has to come now, then return to a de-risked steady state.
caveats: The 80/20 and 4%/64% figures come from the source's own ad account data, not a universal guarantee.
Agencies are often KPI'd on efficiency and profit, which biases them toward CBO and toward squeezing winners short-term.

cards.title: Shift creative mix from desire-led to pain-point-led
cards.summary: Retailers built on campaign shoots skew to desire-led creative; move the mix toward pain-point assets for performance.
cards.use_when: Auditing the creative mix for a fashion, retail or lifestyle store whose account was built from campaign photography
steps: Review your current ad account through a desire-vs-pain lens: count assets that build desire (models, aspirational shots that make people want the product) versus assets that address a customer pain point.
Recognise the source of the skew: campaign shoots only build desire and don't play to pain points at all, so accounts built on them become heavily desire-weighted.

Use the source's recommended target ratio as a starting heuristic: shift toward 60/40 pain-to-desire, with the strongest brands closer to 70/30, treating desire-led assets as the branding-driven portion and pain-led as performance-marketing assets.
Translate this ratio into your next shoot plan: brief additional concepts that open on a concrete customer frustration rather than a look.
The source's rule of thumb: the best performance marketing assets are the ones that sit on pain.
caveats: Ratios are the source's opinion/heuristic for the brands they audit, not an experimentally proven benchmark.
This is aimed particularly at nine-figure large retailers in the source's market; smaller brands may need different mixes.

cards.title: Build bottom-of-funnel ads around buyer objections
cards.summary: Map why non-buyers didn't convert by objection type and produce retargeting creative that handles each one.
cards.use_when: Designing retargeting/BOF creative for a store with an established conversion rate
steps: Start from the maths: at a 5% site conversion rate, 95% didn't buy. List the likely reasons rather than assuming one cause.
Break the non-buyers into objection buckets. The source's example mix: ~20% price, ~20% brand trust, ~20% product quality, ~20% simply not ready yet.

Match creative to each objection: for price, show discounts, value anchoring, or cost-per-use angles (e.g. compare a supplement to the price of a coffee for the same caffeine). For brand trust, use social proof — customer counts, five-star review counts, UGC testimonials. For quality doubts, use UGC of the product in use, before/afters and demonstrations. For 'too soon', stay present with educational or lifestyle content.
Build your BOF asset mix proportionally to whichever objections actually dominate; the source treats objection handling as the primary purpose of a product ad in BOF retargeting.
Repeat the exercise for common high-volume product categories from your order data to make the objection mix accurate.
caveats: The percentages are illustrative examples from the source, not measured distributions in your account.
Price objection buyers may convert later on promotion, not at full price.

cards.title: Volume beats everything only above a quality bar
cards.summary: Prioritise volume, then concept quality, hook strength, editing, UGC talent and storytelling — but only once each ad clears a minimum quality bar.
cards.use_when: Setting the output target and quality standard for your creative pipeline for a store's paid social programme
steps: Rank production priorities in this order: volume first, then concept quality, then hook strength, then editing quality, then UGC talent, then storytelling.
Define what a 7/10 ad looks like for your store: a documented bar covering concept elements, hook elements, and format matched to the stage of awareness.

Judge future ads against that bar. The source's claim is that among ads above the bar, even 10 top creative strategists cannot reliably pick the winner, so don't burn effort trying to predict the top 1%; just produce more ads that clear the bar.
Avoid 'junk volume': the source describes brands pushing thousands of ads a month that lack good concept, hook or awareness-matched format — the volume was real but under the bar.
Reinvest effort continuously into understanding and raising the minimum bar, then maximising volume above it.
caveats: The 7/10 bar is the source's analogy, not a formal rubric.
'Volume matters most' can be misread as licence to ship low-quality ads; the source explicitly warns against that.

cards.title: Two ways to size monthly creative volume
cards.summary: Simple rule: one new ad per $1k monthly spend; better method: back-propagate from new-customer revenue target divided by average expected revenue per ad.
cards.use_when: Setting how many new ads your store needs to produce this month
steps: Quick estimate: produce one new ad per $1,000 of monthly ad spend (e.g. 30k/mo = 30 ads, 50k/mo = 50 ads). The source gives this in AUD and says it translates roughly fine to USD.
Better method: calculate average spend per ad. If you launched 500 ads and spent $500,000 over the last year, each ad averaged $1,000 spent.
Find average return per ad: either acquisition MER (new customer revenue / ad spend) or roROAS on a 7-day click basis. At roROAS 3 and $1,000 mean spend, expected revenue per ad is $3,000.
Back-propagate from target: divide your monthly new customer revenue target by expected revenue per ad. A $300k new-customer-revenue target ÷ $3,000 = 100 creatives per month.
Flex volume with the forecast through the year: as your expected new-customer revenue changes, creative volume should track the same shape.

Account for two gaps in the simple model: average time for an ad to earn its revenue (if it takes 4 months, required volume must be much higher), and the split between winners and losers (100 losing ads generate almost nothing; 100 winners can generate millions). Forecast winners and losers separately and layer the time component in.
caveats: The $1k-per-ad rule is a rough heuristic, not a precision forecast.
The detailed model requires your own historical spend, return and timing data to be meaningful.

cards.title: Set creative production budget as a share of media spend by scale
cards.summary: 4–30k/mo spend: founder-led, time not money; 30–100k: ~25% of media budget to production; 100k+: asymptote to ~10%.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much of the paid social budget to allocate to creative production at your current spend level
steps: At 4–30k/month spend: run founder-led content and statics. Production budget is your time, not cash — the source says statics and founder-led video can get you to 30k/month spend without paid production. The founder should be creating it so they learn the ideation, scripting and editing process and can then KPI and train others.

At 30–100k/month: allocate about 25% of media budget to production (100k/month = 25k/month on creative). The source notes this is far more than most brands spend and is a stated reason many brands fail to scale.
Expect this range to feel uncomfortable — production cost is high relative to the business and feels off, but it democratises at scale.
Above 100k/month: let the percentage fall to around 10% of media budget. As a share of revenue, at 25% MER, 10% of media budget equals roughly 2.5% of total revenue.
Spend that allocation on diversity: UGC, partnership ads, an in-house or part-time static designer, and possibly a low-cost agency for another creative type such as VSSLs.
caveats: Percentages are the source's recommendations from agency practice, not measured industry standards.
Founder-led production at low spend requires genuine founder involvement; outsourcing without learning the craft undercuts the stated benefit.

cards.title: Treat production spend as a revenue driver, not a cost centre
cards.summary: Case example: a 350k/mo brand stuck at 15 ads refused production spend; reworking old winners lifted results, but fatigue eventually reversed them.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to shift a slice of media budget into creative production on a high-spend, low-creative-volume store
steps: Diagnose the bottleneck before optimising media buying: the source describes a brand spending 350k/month with only ~15 live ads, where the media buyer over-segmented into ~25 campaigns and experimented with big caps and cost caps to squeeze those 15 ads, because there was nothing to work with creatively.
First response used here: relaunch and rework old performers still available in the account, taking 15 ads to about 60 without any new creative production.

That alone reportedly raised spend ~40k/month, cut CAC 20–30% and grew new-customer revenue ~28% — but the founder saw Meta spend as revenue-driving and production as a cost centre and refused further production.

Model the reallocation before deciding: the source proposed moving $10k/month from media to production to buy about 40 assets (some hook swaps, some statics) at an agency, roughly doubling active ads, and estimated this would unlock at least a 5% efficiency improvement. On 350k spend, 5% is about 17.5k, so either drop 17.5k of spend (having spent 10k, net ~7k gain) or keep spend flat and gain incremental revenue — at their then-3x return, an extra 40–50k/month.
Watch for the downside: when no new creative arrives, the 60 ads fatigue, ads get turned off, spend redistributes away and the account drifts back toward its previous level.
caveats: All figures come from one client case study and are examples, not promises.
The source's own agency proposed the reallocation, so the recommendation and the case study are not independent.

cards.title: Test bulk creative and hook variants via Instagram trial reels
cards.summary: Post ads as trial reels with the CTA cut off to read viral reach and retention graphs before spending in Ads Manager.
cards.use_when: Validating a batch of new hooks or rough cuts cheaply before loading them into a paid account
steps: Take V1 of an asset and post it as a trial reel from the business or personal page, cutting the in-app CTA off the end.
Read two outputs: comparative reach (does the post travel at all relative to other trial reels) and the retention graph, which shows whether the drop-off is in the hook, bridge or body.

Use this before perfection: if captions or other details still need a round-2 fix, post V1 as a trial reel while round two is being edited, and gather feedback within about 24 hours before the final asset exists.

Use it especially for hook testing at volume: post ~20 hook variations as trial reels, see which retain best, and put only the top ~5 into the ad account instead of paying to test all 20. The source says they do this on all of their own ads.
caveats: The source frames this as tactical and time-sensitive ('as of April 2026') and says it may stop applying as algorithms change. Verify the current trial reel interface before relying on it.
Retention and reach metrics are diagnostics, not proof of conversion performance.

cards.title: Understand total spend capacity and shape the fatigue curve
cards.summary: Every ad has a finite lifetime spend capacity; you can shape the curve to squeeze short-term cash or let high performers breathe longer.
cards.use_when: Deciding how hard to push a winning ad given inventory position, cash conversion cycle and growth rate
steps: Plot the ad's daily spend over time: spend rises as Meta distributes budget (or you raise it), plateaus around a maximum daily spend limit, then fatigues and gets pulled down or turned off. The area under that curve is the ad's total spend capacity.
Accept the two rules: every ad has a total spend capacity, and every ad will fatigue and eventually be turned off.

Choose the curve deliberately. Squeeze option: take the ad to a high daily budget to sell through inventory fast, accepting earlier fatigue and degraded MER. Breathe option: hold the ad at a low daily budget like $100 and aim for months of life rather than weeks.

Choose squeeze when you have inventory that must sell through this month for the P&L position; choose breathe when inventory is short, replenishment is pending, or growth is outrunning your cash conversion cycle.

Give whoever runs your account the wider business context (inventory, cash, growth) — the source warns an agency sees a winner and squeezes it to produce a strong 30–90 day case study and good roROAS reporting, which can ruin long-term account and inventory stability.
caveats: The source is describing agency incentives that may not apply to in-house teams or aligned agencies.
Full derivative modelling of the curve is approximate; use it as a directional decision tool.

cards.title: Diagnose the two causes of creative fatigue
cards.summary: Fatigue comes from the ad itself going stale or from pushing too much spend through too small an audience.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a previously strong ad is losing spend and deciding whether to iterate it or change targeting breadth
steps: Cause one — the ad is stale: it has reached maximum spend capacity, or it repeats the same visuals, concepts and value propositions targeting the same audience as other creatives in the account, which accelerates fatigue. Fix by rotating hooks, changing format, or introducing genuinely different concepts.

Cause two — the audience is too small: a highly specific persona has a maximum daily spend capacity you cannot exceed without driving frequency and wrecking profitability. Example used: creatine for men running sub-4-hour marathons, or in B2B, e-commerce CFOs in Australia running $100m+ businesses — only about 1,000–2,000 people, so $10k/day would hit each of them hundreds of times.

Estimate each persona's spend capacity and park spend there, rotating creative so you can keep hitting the audience as it churns (e.g. people enter a marathon-training audience, run their race, and leave; new people keep entering).

Scale further by widening the callout, not by over-spending on the narrow one: broadening from 'CFO of $100m+ e-commerce business' to 'e-commerce founders earning over 100k' dramatically increases daily spend capacity — but the source warns against going broad reflexively, because broader callouts force you to make better creative that resonates with more people.
Treat the sequencing as: highly specific persona callouts that raise creative quality first, then move broader once you hit scale.
caveats: The source states good top-of-funnel unaware ads are very hard and most brands shouldn't attempt them below roughly $50m+ scale.
Audience-size estimates in the examples are rough figures, not researched counts.

cards.title: Four tactical responses once an ad fatigues
cards.summary: Iterate hooks, move to a cost cap campaign, duplicate ad sets (not recommended), port post IDs to a scaling campaign, or rotate formats.
cards.use_when: Choosing what to do with a fatigued ad instead of simply killing it
steps: Lead with iteration: take a hero ad that has started to fatigue and rotate new hooks onto it to extract more spend from the same asset.

Optionally move the ad into a cost cap campaign to pull more spend through it. The source says this works but fatigues the creative faster and is a short-term media buying tactic that won't materially change the business.
Duplicate ad sets: the source explicitly does not recommend this, calls it too tacky, and says it worked in the past but not now. Include only if you already believe it works.
Move the post ID of the creative into another campaign such as a scaling campaign so it keeps existing engagement. The source says this sometimes works but won't save the account.

Rotate formats as a variation of iteration: translate a strong video into a static, a strong VSSL into UGC, or a strong image into an unaware long-form copy static — the source notes these are quite different strategies.
Accept that these tactics only squeeze a little more from the back end of a creative. The real answer is the portfolio approach: have other performing ads to fall back on.
caveats: The source ranks duplicate ad sets as not recommended and scaling-campaign moves as unreliable.
None of these extend a creative's core capacity; they delay the turn-off.

cards.title: Run media buying as portfolio and inventory management
cards.summary: Above ~50k/month, the media buyer's job is diversifying risk across ads and products and aligning the ad account with commercial objectives, not just maximising profit.
cards.use_when: Reviewing agency or media buyer performance against your actual commercial position (inventory, cash, sell-through)
steps: Above about 50k/month spend, treat the media buyer's core job as portfolio management across ads and products, aligning commercial objectives with what the ad account is doing.
Decide whether you want Pareto concentration in the account or whether to force against it structurally so you're not over-leveraged on a handful of ads. Run the same decision at product level.

Consider the P&L vs balance sheet trade-off: agencies optimise to maximum profit and efficiency because that's what they're KPI'd on, which can mean failing to sell through inventory. The source's example: a business with $2m profit on the P&L and $3m of unsold inventory on the balance sheet is negative $1m in cash.

If you're in that position, restructure the account to sell through stock even though returns and efficiency won't be optimal and you'll have to make creative around that stock — the source frames it as a hard pill that rebalances the business.
Make sure whoever runs your media is across your inventory position; the source states plainly that if the media buyer isn't across inventory, that isn't good.
caveats: The ~50k/month threshold is the source's heuristic.
Optimising for sell-through can visibly worsen reported efficiency, so expectations need to be set with whoever owns the P&L.

cards.title: Split production effort across replication, iteration and net-new
cards.summary: Prioritise reproduction of winners most heavily, then iteration on near-misses, then net-new concepts — roughly 50–60/20–30/20–30.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to point your creative team's production hours each month
steps: Classify each planned asset into one of three types. Winning content replication: repeat or lightly rework assets that already worked (hook iterations, format translations, reposting strong organic). The source calls this by far the highest-impact content type for both paid and organic — reposting proven assets reaches new audiences repeatedly. Iterative content: fix underperformers via hook or format changes, or take a working concept to a new persona or a new offer. Net-new concepts: entirely new formats, angles and concepts.
Allocate roughly 50–60% of effort to replication, 20–30% to iteration and 20–30% to net-new, adjusting for performance and risk profile.
Do not allocate 0% to net-new: everything up the chain eventually fatigues and falls off, so new concepts must keep flowing up to feed replication.

Correct for your own bias: the source admits their organic content runs about 80–90% net-new and only 10–20% replication, and that replication consistently holds around 80% of views — evidence of overallocation to net-new.
caveats: The percentage split is the source's general recommendation and explicitly changes by business context.
The 80%-of-views figure is from the source's own organic content, not a universal result.

cards.title: Brief creators properly and vet them via their prior briefs
cards.summary: Creator output quality is a product of your brief quality; vet creators by comparing past work to the brief behind it.
cards.use_when: Sourcing UGC creators or briefing in-house video for a store's ad scripts
steps: Before hiring, collect examples of the creator's past output — the source calls skipping this self-evidently bad.

Also request the brief behind each example. Comparing output against brief tells you how much scaffolding they need: if they produced something excellent from a terrible brief, you can send broad strokes; if the brief was extremely in-depth, you should match that level of detail.
Write the highest-quality, most in-depth brief you can for the highest output quality.
Don't force script adherence: ask for one take held to the script and one that feels more natural, then choose the better or run both.

Check regional fit separately: creators must be native to the market you're targeting. The source says an Australian accent translated into the US market underperforms, US creatives need native US accents, and UK-to-AU translates decently but native still wins. The script can be identical — only the local creator changes.
If you also post organic content that performs well, reuse it rather than only producing new material, since repeated posts reach people who haven't seen them.
caveats: The accent/market guidance is the source's observation from their own account experience, not a researched benchmark.
An in-depth brief is recommended but must be paired with a creator who can execute it.

cards.title: Where AI helps and hurts in the creative pipeline
cards.summary: Automate briefing/scripting and production heavily with AI, keep human judgement in ideation and analysis.
cards.use_when: Deciding which creative workflow steps to hand to AI for a store's ad production
steps: Map the pipeline: ideation → briefing → production → publishing → analysis feeding back into ideation.

Do not automate ideation. The source's reasoning is that LLMs converge on the same outputs, so no amount of context, documentation, Reddit scraping or custom skills produces ideas differentiated from competitors. A creative strategist still has to validate concepting here.

Automate briefing and script writing heavily. Build a branded AI skill that walks through a questionnaire — who is the persona, what's the concept, what's the offer, long form or short, which stage of awareness — and outputs a brief or script said to be 99% of the way there, needing a ~1% tweak.
Automate production as far as the format allows. The source says VSSLs and static image ads can be about 90% AI-produced, and AI is native to the video editor role more broadly.

Be careful with AI in analysis: it won't respect your metric hierarchy and won't weight account structure or commercial context properly. The source says they use it in analysis but that it misses often and can actively point you in the wrong direction if used for core decisions.
The principle: skip automating the outer ends of the pipeline and maximise throughput in the middle (briefing and production).
caveats: The '99% there' and '90% AI' figures are the source's experience, not measured benchmarks.
The statement that LLM ideation always converges on the same output is the source's opinion at time of recording and may change as tools evolve.

cards.title: Hire and incentivise a creative strategist
cards.summary: Creative strategy is primarily copywriting; source candidates from copywriters, other brands, or promote designers/editors, and consider a 3%-of-ad-spend variable.
cards.use_when: Building or restructuring the production team behind a store's paid social creative
steps: Fill three core roles: a video editor for video ads (AI-native strongly preferred, since it unlocks more assets and footage that doesn't yet exist), a designer for statics (both roles can be global, part-time outcome-based contractors or full-time), and a creative strategist.

Look for the strategist in this order: copywriters, because creative strategy is primarily copywriting — writing scripts, writing static briefs, ideating new personas — and LLMs have made the drafting part of copywriting less scarce, so the ideation is the valuable part. Alternatively, poach an existing creative strategist or backfill from your designer or video editor, which shortens the feedback loop because the same person can ideate, design and brief edits.
Understand the workflow you're hiring into: the strategist brings ideas and moves them into a branded AI skill that outputs the actual script for production.

Consider a variable component tied to results: the source describes paying creative strategists roughly 3% of ad spend based on the creatives they produce and brief, so they're directly incentivised to maximise hit rates.

Judge the model by scale: the source reports this works well on mid-size brands, but at very large spend a strategist could earn around $80,000 a month, at which point the model breaks and brands move away from it.
caveats: The 3% and $80,000/month figures are the source's observations of a practice, not standard rates.
The source notes creative strategist is a new role with few experienced candidates in market.

cards.title: Start organic content before paid for small stores
cards.summary: Organic forces you to learn what content people actually watch, which compounds into paid creative quality.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a small or early-stage store should invest in organic before or alongside Meta spend
steps: Run the source's recommendation for smaller founders: post organically every single day and get good at identifying what good content looks like, rather than assuming paid comes first.
Watch what actually gains views and study retention graphs plus share and save rates — these teach you what holds attention.

The stated reason isn't that organic outperforms paid, but that organic forces you to become good at creative, and that skill compounds into paid ads when you know how to make content people want to watch.
Where you reuse organic output in paid, favour repetition of proven pieces: repeat the same content over and over, because every repetition reaches a new audience and tends to perform similarly.
Pair this with format discipline: identify the awareness stage of the piece and match the format to it, then move validated concepts from statics into video.
caveats: This is the source's forward-looking recommendation for 2026–2027, not a measured result.
Daily posting requires sustained founder or team time; it is a discipline commitment rather than a shortcut.

If those few ads fatigue, you have no backups.","Choose CBO if you need a quick efficiency spike and don't care about de-risking or testing right now.","Choose ABO-style manual control if you want a lower-risk steady state, more ads and products working, and protection against a single fatigue event.","For stores with a large product portfolio, avoid putting all products under one CBO, because spend concentrates into a few products (Pareto applies at product level too) and skews your assortment.","Note the source's own preference: they lean toward the lower-risk structure most of the time but switch to CBO in periods where efficiency has to come now, then return to a de-risked steady state."],"caveats":["The 80/20 and 4%/64% figures come from the source's own ad account data, not a universal guarantee.","Agencies are often KPI'd on efficiency and profit, which biases them toward CBO and toward squeezing winners short-term."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","facebook-ads","campaign-structure","cbo","media-buying","risk-management","product-portfolio"]},{"title":"Shift creative mix from desire-led to pain-point-led","summary":"Retailers built on campaign shoots skew to desire-led creative; move the mix toward pain-point assets for performance.","use_when":"Auditing the creative mix for a fashion, retail or lifestyle store whose account was built from campaign photography","steps":["Review your current ad account through a desire-vs-pain lens: count assets that build desire (models, aspirational shots that make people want the product) versus assets that address a customer pain point.","Recognise the source of the skew: campaign shoots only build desire and don't play to pain points at all, so accounts built on them become heavily desire-weighted.","Use the source's recommended target ratio as a starting heuristic: shift toward 60/40 pain-to-desire, with the strongest brands closer to 70/30, treating desire-led assets as the branding-driven portion and pain-led as performance-marketing assets.","Translate this ratio into your next shoot plan: brief additional concepts that open on a concrete customer frustration rather than a look.","The source's rule of thumb: the best performance marketing assets are the ones that sit on pain."],"caveats":["Ratios are the source's opinion/heuristic for the brands they audit, not an experimentally proven benchmark.","This is aimed particularly at nine-figure large retailers in the source's market; smaller brands may need different mixes."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-strategy","customer-research","positioning","retail","ad-creative","messaging"]},{"title":"Build bottom-of-funnel ads around buyer objections","summary":"Map why non-buyers didn't convert by objection type and produce retargeting creative that handles each one.","use_when":"Designing retargeting/BOF creative for a store with an established conversion rate","steps":["Start from the maths: at a 5% site conversion rate, 95% didn't buy. List the likely reasons rather than assuming one cause.","Break the non-buyers into objection buckets. The source's example mix: ~20% price, ~20% brand trust, ~20% product quality, ~20% simply not ready yet.","Match creative to each objection: for price, show discounts, value anchoring, or cost-per-use angles (e.g. compare a supplement to the price of a coffee for the same caffeine). For brand trust, use social proof — customer counts, five-star review counts, UGC testimonials. For quality doubts, use UGC of the product in use, before/afters and demonstrations. For 'too soon', stay present with educational or lifestyle content.","Build your BOF asset mix proportionally to whichever objections actually dominate; the source treats objection handling as the primary purpose of a product ad in BOF retargeting.","Repeat the exercise for common high-volume product categories from your order data to make the objection mix accurate."],"caveats":["The percentages are illustrative examples from the source, not measured distributions in your account.","Price objection buyers may convert later on promotion, not at full price."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","retargeting","bottom-of-funnel","creative-strategy","social-proof","ugc","conversion-optimization"]},{"title":"Volume beats everything only above a quality bar","summary":"Prioritise volume, then concept quality, hook strength, editing, UGC talent and storytelling — but only once each ad clears a minimum quality bar.","use_when":"Setting the output target and quality standard for your creative pipeline for a store's paid social programme","steps":["Rank production priorities in this order: volume first, then concept quality, then hook strength, then editing quality, then UGC talent, then storytelling.","Define what a 7/10 ad looks like for your store: a documented bar covering concept elements, hook elements, and format matched to the stage of awareness.","Judge future ads against that bar. The source's claim is that among ads above the bar, even 10 top creative strategists cannot reliably pick the winner, so don't burn effort trying to predict the top 1%; just produce more ads that clear the bar.","Avoid 'junk volume': the source describes brands pushing thousands of ads a month that lack good concept, hook or awareness-matched format — the volume was real but under the bar.","Reinvest effort continuously into understanding and raising the minimum bar, then maximising volume above it."],"caveats":["The 7/10 bar is the source's analogy, not a formal rubric.","'Volume matters most' can be misread as licence to ship low-quality ads; the source explicitly warns against that."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-strategy","ad-creative","creative-testing","production","process-design"]},{"title":"Two ways to size monthly creative volume","summary":"Simple rule: one new ad per $1k monthly spend; better method: back-propagate from new-customer revenue target divided by average expected revenue per ad.","use_when":"Setting how many new ads your store needs to produce this month","steps":["Quick estimate: produce one new ad per $1,000 of monthly ad spend (e.g. 30k/mo = 30 ads, 50k/mo = 50 ads). The source gives this in AUD and says it translates roughly fine to USD.","Better method: calculate average spend per ad. If you launched 500 ads and spent $500,000 over the last year, each ad averaged $1,000 spent.","Find average return per ad: either acquisition MER (new customer revenue / ad spend) or roROAS on a 7-day click basis. At roROAS 3 and $1,000 mean spend, expected revenue per ad is $3,000.","Back-propagate from target: divide your monthly new customer revenue target by expected revenue per ad. A $300k new-customer-revenue target ÷ $3,000 = 100 creatives per month.","Flex volume with the forecast through the year: as your expected new-customer revenue changes, creative volume should track the same shape.","Account for two gaps in the simple model: average time for an ad to earn its revenue (if it takes 4 months, required volume must be much higher), and the split between winners and losers (100 losing ads generate almost nothing; 100 winners can generate millions). Forecast winners and losers separately and layer the time component in."],"caveats":["The $1k-per-ad rule is a rough heuristic, not a precision forecast.","The detailed model requires your own historical spend, return and timing data to be meaningful."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-production","forecasting","budgeting","measurement","acquisition","media-buying"]},{"title":"Set creative production budget as a share of media spend by scale","summary":"4–30k/mo spend: founder-led, time not money; 30–100k: ~25% of media budget to production; 100k+: asymptote to ~10%.","use_when":"Deciding how much of the paid social budget to allocate to creative production at your current spend level","steps":["At 4–30k/month spend: run founder-led content and statics. Production budget is your time, not cash — the source says statics and founder-led video can get you to 30k/month spend without paid production. The founder should be creating it so they learn the ideation, scripting and editing process and can then KPI and train others.","At 30–100k/month: allocate about 25% of media budget to production (100k/month = 25k/month on creative). The source notes this is far more than most brands spend and is a stated reason many brands fail to scale.","Expect this range to feel uncomfortable — production cost is high relative to the business and feels off, but it democratises at scale.","Above 100k/month: let the percentage fall to around 10% of media budget. As a share of revenue, at 25% MER, 10% of media budget equals roughly 2.5% of total revenue.","Spend that allocation on diversity: UGC, partnership ads, an in-house or part-time static designer, and possibly a low-cost agency for another creative type such as VSSLs."],"caveats":["Percentages are the source's recommendations from agency practice, not measured industry standards.","Founder-led production at low spend requires genuine founder involvement; outsourcing without learning the craft undercuts the stated benefit."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-production","budgeting","founder-led-content","production-team","media-buying","scale"]},{"title":"Treat production spend as a revenue driver, not a cost centre","summary":"Case example: a 350k/mo brand stuck at 15 ads refused production spend; reworking old winners lifted results, but fatigue eventually reversed them.","use_when":"Deciding whether to shift a slice of media budget into creative production on a high-spend, low-creative-volume store","steps":["Diagnose the bottleneck before optimising media buying: the source describes a brand spending 350k/month with only ~15 live ads, where the media buyer over-segmented into ~25 campaigns and experimented with big caps and cost caps to squeeze those 15 ads, because there was nothing to work with creatively.","First response used here: relaunch and rework old performers still available in the account, taking 15 ads to about 60 without any new creative production.","That alone reportedly raised spend ~40k/month, cut CAC 20–30% and grew new-customer revenue ~28% — but the founder saw Meta spend as revenue-driving and production as a cost centre and refused further production.","Model the reallocation before deciding: the source proposed moving $10k/month from media to production to buy about 40 assets (some hook swaps, some statics) at an agency, roughly doubling active ads, and estimated this would unlock at least a 5% efficiency improvement. On 350k spend, 5% is about 17.5k, so either drop 17.5k of spend (having spent 10k, net ~7k gain) or keep spend flat and gain incremental revenue — at their then-3x return, an extra 40–50k/month.","Watch for the downside: when no new creative arrives, the 60 ads fatigue, ads get turned off, spend redistributes away and the account drifts back toward its previous level."],"caveats":["All figures come from one client case study and are examples, not promises.","The source's own agency proposed the reallocation, so the recommendation and the case study are not independent."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-production","budgeting","media-buying","scale","case-study","cac"]},{"title":"Test bulk creative and hook variants via Instagram trial reels","summary":"Post ads as trial reels with the CTA cut off to read viral reach and retention graphs before spending in Ads Manager.","use_when":"Validating a batch of new hooks or rough cuts cheaply before loading them into a paid account","steps":["Take V1 of an asset and post it as a trial reel from the business or personal page, cutting the in-app CTA off the end.","Read two outputs: comparative reach (does the post travel at all relative to other trial reels) and the retention graph, which shows whether the drop-off is in the hook, bridge or body.","Use this before perfection: if captions or other details still need a round-2 fix, post V1 as a trial reel while round two is being edited, and gather feedback within about 24 hours before the final asset exists.","Use it especially for hook testing at volume: post ~20 hook variations as trial reels, see which retain best, and put only the top ~5 into the ad account instead of paying to test all 20. The source says they do this on all of their own ads."],"caveats":["The source frames this as tactical and time-sensitive ('as of April 2026') and says it may stop applying as algorithms change. Verify the current trial reel interface before relying on it.","Retention and reach metrics are diagnostics, not proof of conversion performance."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-testing","instagram","trial-reels","hook-testing","retention","experiment-design"]},{"title":"Understand total spend capacity and shape the fatigue curve","summary":"Every ad has a finite lifetime spend capacity; you can shape the curve to squeeze short-term cash or let high performers breathe longer.","use_when":"Deciding how hard to push a winning ad given inventory position, cash conversion cycle and growth rate","steps":["Plot the ad's daily spend over time: spend rises as Meta distributes budget (or you raise it), plateaus around a maximum daily spend limit, then fatigues and gets pulled down or turned off. The area under that curve is the ad's total spend capacity.","Accept the two rules: every ad has a total spend capacity, and every ad will fatigue and eventually be turned off.","Choose the curve deliberately. Squeeze option: take the ad to a high daily budget to sell through inventory fast, accepting earlier fatigue and degraded MER. Breathe option: hold the ad at a low daily budget like $100 and aim for months of life rather than weeks.","Choose squeeze when you have inventory that must sell through this month for the P&L position; choose breathe when inventory is short, replenishment is pending, or growth is outrunning your cash conversion cycle.","Give whoever runs your account the wider business context (inventory, cash, growth) — the source warns an agency sees a winner and squeezes it to produce a strong 30–90 day case study and good roROAS reporting, which can ruin long-term account and inventory stability."],"caveats":["The source is describing agency incentives that may not apply to in-house teams or aligned agencies.","Full derivative modelling of the curve is approximate; use it as a directional decision tool."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-fatigue","media-buying","inventory","cash-flow","scaling","agency-management"]},{"title":"Diagnose the two causes of creative fatigue","summary":"Fatigue comes from the ad itself going stale or from pushing too much spend through too small an audience.","use_when":"Diagnosing why a previously strong ad is losing spend and deciding whether to iterate it or change targeting breadth","steps":["Cause one — the ad is stale: it has reached maximum spend capacity, or it repeats the same visuals, concepts and value propositions targeting the same audience as other creatives in the account, which accelerates fatigue. Fix by rotating hooks, changing format, or introducing genuinely different concepts.","Cause two — the audience is too small: a highly specific persona has a maximum daily spend capacity you cannot exceed without driving frequency and wrecking profitability. Example used: creatine for men running sub-4-hour marathons, or in B2B, e-commerce CFOs in Australia running $100m+ businesses — only about 1,000–2,000 people, so $10k/day would hit each of them hundreds of times.","Estimate each persona's spend capacity and park spend there, rotating creative so you can keep hitting the audience as it churns (e.g. people enter a marathon-training audience, run their race, and leave; new people keep entering).","Scale further by widening the callout, not by over-spending on the narrow one: broadening from 'CFO of $100m+ e-commerce business' to 'e-commerce founders earning over 100k' dramatically increases daily spend capacity — but the source warns against going broad reflexively, because broader callouts force you to make better creative that resonates with more people.","Treat the sequencing as: highly specific persona callouts that raise creative quality first, then move broader once you hit scale."],"caveats":["The source states good top-of-funnel unaware ads are very hard and most brands shouldn't attempt them below roughly $50m+ scale.","Audience-size estimates in the examples are rough figures, not researched counts."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-fatigue","audience-targeting","personas","frequency","scaling","ad-creative"]},{"title":"Four tactical responses once an ad fatigues","summary":"Iterate hooks, move to a cost cap campaign, duplicate ad sets (not recommended), port post IDs to a scaling campaign, or rotate formats.","use_when":"Choosing what to do with a fatigued ad instead of simply killing it","steps":["Lead with iteration: take a hero ad that has started to fatigue and rotate new hooks onto it to extract more spend from the same asset.","Optionally move the ad into a cost cap campaign to pull more spend through it. The source says this works but fatigues the creative faster and is a short-term media buying tactic that won't materially change the business.","Duplicate ad sets: the source explicitly does not recommend this, calls it too tacky, and says it worked in the past but not now. Include only if you already believe it works.","Move the post ID of the creative into another campaign such as a scaling campaign so it keeps existing engagement. The source says this sometimes works but won't save the account.","Rotate formats as a variation of iteration: translate a strong video into a static, a strong VSSL into UGC, or a strong image into an unaware long-form copy static — the source notes these are quite different strategies.","Accept that these tactics only squeeze a little more from the back end of a creative. The real answer is the portfolio approach: have other performing ads to fall back on."],"caveats":["The source ranks duplicate ad sets as not recommended and scaling-campaign moves as unreliable.","None of these extend a creative's core capacity; they delay the turn-off."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-fatigue","media-buying","ad-creative","format-rotation","scaling","cost-cap"]},{"title":"Run media buying as portfolio and inventory management","summary":"Above ~50k/month, the media buyer's job is diversifying risk across ads and products and aligning the ad account with commercial objectives, not just maximising profit.","use_when":"Reviewing agency or media buyer performance against your actual commercial position (inventory, cash, sell-through)","steps":["Above about 50k/month spend, treat the media buyer's core job as portfolio management across ads and products, aligning commercial objectives with what the ad account is doing.","Decide whether you want Pareto concentration in the account or whether to force against it structurally so you're not over-leveraged on a handful of ads. Run the same decision at product level.","Consider the P&L vs balance sheet trade-off: agencies optimise to maximum profit and efficiency because that's what they're KPI'd on, which can mean failing to sell through inventory. The source's example: a business with $2m profit on the P&L and $3m of unsold inventory on the balance sheet is negative $1m in cash.","If you're in that position, restructure the account to sell through stock even though returns and efficiency won't be optimal and you'll have to make creative around that stock — the source frames it as a hard pill that rebalances the business.","Make sure whoever runs your media is across your inventory position; the source states plainly that if the media buyer isn't across inventory, that isn't good."],"caveats":["The ~50k/month threshold is the source's heuristic.","Optimising for sell-through can visibly worsen reported efficiency, so expectations need to be set with whoever owns the P&L."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","media-buying","inventory","profitability","portfolio-management","agency-management","sell-through"]},{"title":"Split production effort across replication, iteration and net-new","summary":"Prioritise reproduction of winners most heavily, then iteration on near-misses, then net-new concepts — roughly 50–60/20–30/20–30.","use_when":"Deciding where to point your creative team's production hours each month","steps":["Classify each planned asset into one of three types. Winning content replication: repeat or lightly rework assets that already worked (hook iterations, format translations, reposting strong organic). The source calls this by far the highest-impact content type for both paid and organic — reposting proven assets reaches new audiences repeatedly. Iterative content: fix underperformers via hook or format changes, or take a working concept to a new persona or a new offer. Net-new concepts: entirely new formats, angles and concepts.","Allocate roughly 50–60% of effort to replication, 20–30% to iteration and 20–30% to net-new, adjusting for performance and risk profile.","Do not allocate 0% to net-new: everything up the chain eventually fatigues and falls off, so new concepts must keep flowing up to feed replication.","Correct for your own bias: the source admits their organic content runs about 80–90% net-new and only 10–20% replication, and that replication consistently holds around 80% of views — evidence of overallocation to net-new."],"caveats":["The percentage split is the source's general recommendation and explicitly changes by business context.","The 80%-of-views figure is from the source's own organic content, not a universal result."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","creative-production","content-strategy","process-design","iteration","organic-content","resource-allocation"]},{"title":"Brief creators properly and vet them via their prior briefs","summary":"Creator output quality is a product of your brief quality; vet creators by comparing past work to the brief behind it.","use_when":"Sourcing UGC creators or briefing in-house video for a store's ad scripts","steps":["Before hiring, collect examples of the creator's past output — the source calls skipping this self-evidently bad.","Also request the brief behind each example. Comparing output against brief tells you how much scaffolding they need: if they produced something excellent from a terrible brief, you can send broad strokes; if the brief was extremely in-depth, you should match that level of detail.","Write the highest-quality, most in-depth brief you can for the highest output quality.","Don't force script adherence: ask for one take held to the script and one that feels more natural, then choose the better or run both.","Check regional fit separately: creators must be native to the market you're targeting. The source says an Australian accent translated into the US market underperforms, US creatives need native US accents, and UK-to-AU translates decently but native still wins. The script can be identical — only the local creator changes.","If you also post organic content that performs well, reuse it rather than only producing new material, since repeated posts reach people who haven't seen them."],"caveats":["The accent/market guidance is the source's observation from their own account experience, not a researched benchmark.","An in-depth brief is recommended but must be paired with a creator who can execute it."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","ugc","creative-brief","creator-sourcing","production-team","localisation","ad-creative"]},{"title":"Where AI helps and hurts in the creative pipeline","summary":"Automate briefing/scripting and production heavily with AI, keep human judgement in ideation and analysis.","use_when":"Deciding which creative workflow steps to hand to AI for a store's ad production","steps":["Map the pipeline: ideation → briefing → production → publishing → analysis feeding back into ideation.","Do not automate ideation. The source's reasoning is that LLMs converge on the same outputs, so no amount of context, documentation, Reddit scraping or custom skills produces ideas differentiated from competitors. A creative strategist still has to validate concepting here.","Automate briefing and script writing heavily. Build a branded AI skill that walks through a questionnaire — who is the persona, what's the concept, what's the offer, long form or short, which stage of awareness — and outputs a brief or script said to be 99% of the way there, needing a ~1% tweak.","Automate production as far as the format allows. The source says VSSLs and static image ads can be about 90% AI-produced, and AI is native to the video editor role more broadly.","Be careful with AI in analysis: it won't respect your metric hierarchy and won't weight account structure or commercial context properly. The source says they use it in analysis but that it misses often and can actively point you in the wrong direction if used for core decisions.","The principle: skip automating the outer ends of the pipeline and maximise throughput in the middle (briefing and production)."],"caveats":["The '99% there' and '90% AI' figures are the source's experience, not measured benchmarks.","The statement that LLM ideation always converges on the same output is the source's opinion at time of recording and may change as tools evolve."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","ai","creative-production","creative-brief","workflow","ideation","creative-strategy"]},{"title":"Hire and incentivise a creative strategist","summary":"Creative strategy is primarily copywriting; source candidates from copywriters, other brands, or promote designers/editors, and consider a 3%-of-ad-spend variable.","use_when":"Building or restructuring the production team behind a store's paid social creative","steps":["Fill three core roles: a video editor for video ads (AI-native strongly preferred, since it unlocks more assets and footage that doesn't yet exist), a designer for statics (both roles can be global, part-time outcome-based contractors or full-time), and a creative strategist.","Look for the strategist in this order: copywriters, because creative strategy is primarily copywriting — writing scripts, writing static briefs, ideating new personas — and LLMs have made the drafting part of copywriting less scarce, so the ideation is the valuable part. Alternatively, poach an existing creative strategist or backfill from your designer or video editor, which shortens the feedback loop because the same person can ideate, design and brief edits.","Understand the workflow you're hiring into: the strategist brings ideas and moves them into a branded AI skill that outputs the actual script for production.","Consider a variable component tied to results: the source describes paying creative strategists roughly 3% of ad spend based on the creatives they produce and brief, so they're directly incentivised to maximise hit rates.","Judge the model by scale: the source reports this works well on mid-size brands, but at very large spend a strategist could earn around $80,000 a month, at which point the model breaks and brands move away from it."],"caveats":["The 3% and $80,000/month figures are the source's observations of a practice, not standard rates.","The source notes creative strategist is a new role with few experienced candidates in market."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","production-team","hiring","incentives","creative-strategy","copywriting","agency-management"]},{"title":"Start organic content before paid for small stores","summary":"Organic forces you to learn what content people actually watch, which compounds into paid creative quality.","use_when":"Deciding whether a small or early-stage store should invest in organic before or alongside Meta spend","steps":["Run the source's recommendation for smaller founders: post organically every single day and get good at identifying what good content looks like, rather than assuming paid comes first.","Watch what actually gains views and study retention graphs plus share and save rates — these teach you what holds attention.","The stated reason isn't that organic outperforms paid, but that organic forces you to become good at creative, and that skill compounds into paid ads when you know how to make content people want to watch.","Where you reuse organic output in paid, favour repetition of proven pieces: repeat the same content over and over, because every repetition reaches a new audience and tends to perform similarly.","Pair this with format discipline: identify the awareness stage of the piece and match the format to it, then move validated concepts from statics into video."],"caveats":["This is the source's forward-looking recommendation for 2026–2027, not a measured result.","Daily posting requires sustained founder or team time; it is a discipline commitment rather than a shortcut."],"tags":["paid-social-creative","organic-content","content-strategy","creative-strategy","awareness-stages","format-rotation","audience-research"]}]}

If it's not hitting KPI, and this is way underperforming, go for your life. Do whatever you want. You can turn ads off. It doesn't matter cuz yes, you're going to break some sequencing, but the sequencing isn't working. So, who cares? Go and launch as many ads as you want in here, right? Do whatever you want cuz it's not a KPI. So, you need to change something. But if things are working, definitely don't go and launch more ads in here.

 If you go and make more ads for this concept, let's say the concept's crashing it, so you go and make 20 more ads, go and launch another ad set, right? And call it concept one and then like shoot two or obviously whatever naming convention you want to use to be able to clarify the difference between these, but then also be able to filter that they are the same concept. Now the question becomes, well, how do you scale? Let's say concept one is performing well. What do we do? Well, number one, increase budgets. Never turn this off. A big mistake that people make is they take something that's winning and they turn it off and they go and launch it in like a scaling campaign. There's such a rookie mistake just fundamentally speaking because if something works, don't touch it. Leave it. Increase the budget. Now, in addition to that, sure, you can take these post IDs and you can wrap them around into a scaling campaign. That's fine. And that will work. It works in a lot of accounts. We run scaling campaigns in a lot of accounts. A lot of accounts, we don't run scaling campaigns. Once again, it's dependent on the actual ad account in the business. You can run a scaling campaign. You can take these, you can post them over here. If it doesn't work, don't do it. Just keep it in the testing. And then next to these two, the only third campaign that I would usually recommend is to have a retargeting campaign that is generally on existing customers. So it gives you the ability to exclude existing customers from here and exclude existing customers from here. So these can purely be called and that allows you to control budgets. Depending on how long the customer journey is as well, you might want an adset here on 90-day website visitors as a midfunnel. But this is only if you think that you need to increase frequency on engaged audiences. Now, what are the metrics that matter for being able to measure the performance of creative? Let's list them out in order of reliability. Number one is amount spent. Now, this is counterintuitive. A lot of people look at this and go, why would budget distribution to an ad be the most important proxy for performance over extended time periods? And the reason being is due to the sequencing that we talked about before, right? So, if you have a bunch of different ads, attribution is only going to go to the last ad. So, if we use rorowaz as the primary KPI, we're going to miss the fact that Meta is actually putting all your budget here. Why when this only has a 1.7 and this has a 2.2, why would all the budget go here? Probably because this ad is causing purchases elsewhere in the account. And so, this is actually a great topfunnel asset that likely has a low frequency that's cutting through on new audiences. And so, if you're going to look at these three ads, I would say that this is the highest performer if it has double the spend of the other ones. Even though this is a higher row, sure, but if this could scale, it would have more spend in it. and it doesn't. And so amount spent becomes the best proxy for performance when looking at creative. Number two, sure, is rorowaz or CPA. You just want to be making sure you're looking at 7-day click or incremental attribution. Number three is going to be CPC and CTRs. This is a leading indicator for the effectiveness of the ad. Obviously, you can have good CTRs and good CPCs, but the conversion rate of the ad can suck and it's not a good ad. And so this obviously isn't a primary indicator of the quality of a creative. That is where you have to use multiple different metrics in conjunction to be able to assess quality.
